explanation: Pimozide can increase the QTc interval and potentially cause arrhythmia or sudden death, especially in combination with drugs that raise its levels. Because of its effects on the QTc interval, pimozide is not intended for use unless other options for tic disorders or psychotic disorders have failed. The prevalence of agranulocytosis during clozapine treatment is 0.4%, lower than previously thought and risk of death resulting from this is 0.05%: a rare event. Over 80% of cases of agranulocytosis with clozapine develop within the first 18 weeks of treatment.

Neuropathology The subtypes of dementia are associated with abnormal molecules accumulating in the cerebrum. Which of the following molecules are most likely be found in the below types of dementia? 1. Mrs. Gasker is a 72-year-old woman who has attended her GP as her family is increasingly worried about her ability to manage at home due to cognitive problems, although her memory appears to be intact. They have also noted that she has been experiencing tremor and limb stiffness. She has started to have falls in the last few weeks. (Please choose TWO answers)

2. Mrs. Hunter is a 76-year-old woman who has been exhibiting increasingly odd behaviour over the past 18 months. Her family describe her as being "sensitive" and "diligent" but she has started to make lewd jokes and indifferent to the concerns of others. Her husband has noted that she is finding it difficult to look after herself properly. Please choose ONE option.
correctAnswer: 1) Mrs. Gasker - Alpha-synuclein protein, Ubiquitin 2) Mrs. Hunter - Tau protein
explanation: 1) The first case describes a history of dementia with Lewy bodies. The key constituent of Lewy bodies is alpha-synuclein. When aggregates of misfolded, overexpressed alpha-synuclein accumulate in neurons (axonal processes and synapses) or surrounding glial cells, Lewy bodies are formed. Lewy bodies are immunoreactive for alpha-synuclein as well as for ubiquitin and alpha-beta-crystallin. Neuropathic changes of dementia with Lewy bodies include the presence of Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites in the cerebral cortex as well as in the brainstem. These are often accompanied by some degree of Alzheimer disease neuropathologic changes, often with a moderate beta-amyloid plaque burden but relatively lower tangle burden. 2) The second case describes an example of fronto-temporal dementia. This is associated with tau protein deposition, particularly in Pick's disease. Pick disease is characterised by the presence of Pick bodies: rounded, homogeneous neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions, faintly visible on H&E staining. Immunohistochemical staining shows that these inclusions contain 3Rtau. Pick bodies are also strongly argyrophilic with the Bielschowsky technique.
reference: Sanford AM. Lewy body dementia. Clinics in geriatric medicine. 2018 Nov 1;34(4):603-15. Gray F, Duyckaerts C, de Girolami U. Escourolle and Poirier’s Manual of Basic Neuropathology, 6 th Edition. 2019. pp. 6-7, 192-193, 197.

Theme- Erikson’s stages of development Ego integrity vs. despair Lead In: Which of the following from Erikson’s stages of development apply to each of the below scenarios?

1. Emily Anderson is a 7-year-old girl who was pleased at being praised for working hard at school.

2. Mrs Joan Bakewell is a 70-year-old woman who feels content with her life, despite failing health, past difficulties and an increased level of physical disability.

3. Mr. Elon Musk, aged 47, gives a speech at a graduation ceremony and refers to "making his mark" on the world through creating or nurturing things that will outlast him.
correctAnswer:
1. Emily Anderson - Industry vs. inferiority

2. Mrs Joan Bakewell - Ego integrity vs. despair 3. Mr Elon Musk - Generativity vs. stagnation
explanation: Erik Erikson created an original and highly influential theory of psychological development and crisis occurring in periods that extended across the entire life cycle. Stage 4 takes place from about 5 years to about 13 years. Its focus is industry versus inferiority. The child develops industry by learning new skills and takes pride in the things made. A child unprepared for this stage of psychosocial development, either through an insufficient resolution of previous stages or by current interference, may develop a sense of inferiority and inadequacy. Stage 7 takes place from about 40 years to about 60 years. Its focus is generativity versus stagnation. Generativity encompasses a protective concern for generations and social institutions, as well as productivity and creativity. The last and 8 th stage – integrity versus despair – takes place from about 60 years until death. Erikson defined integrity as “the acceptance of one’s one and only life cycle and of the persons who have become significant to it as something that had to be and that, by necessity, permitted of no substitutions.”
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 1071-1076.

Mr. Harry Dresden is a 62-year-old man who has recently been diagnosed with a depressive episode and has been started on Fluoxetine. Since starting it he has been experiencing nausea, vomiting, muscle cramps and marked lethargy.

2. Mr. Edward Rankin is a 50-year-old man with a diagnosis of bipolar affective disorder who has been stable on Lithium for the past 20 years. He has recently been brought to the GP with limb and joint pains, lethargy, problems with his memory and drinking and urinating large amounts of fluid. He insists that he feels unwell physically but fine in his mood.

3. Mr. Trevor Innes is a 48-year-old man with a long history of alcohol dependence. He had informed his family that he had been troubled by back pain over the last few weeks, but has been presenting as lethargic, nauseous and confused over the past few days.
correctAnswer: 1. Mr. Harry Dresden - Hyponatraemia 2. Mr. Edward Rankin - Hypercalcaemia 3. Mr. Trevor Innes - Uraemia
explanation: 1) This is most likely to represent hyponatraemia which is a relatively common side-effect of most antidepressant varieties, particularly in older populations. 2) This is most likely to be hypercalcaemia, which is more prevalent in individuals taking lithium for a long duration. This electrolyte change results from secondary hyperparathyroidism (i.e. due to the effect of Lithium on the parathyroid glands) although Lithium induced hypercalcaemia can also occur with normal parathyroid levels. Hypercalcaemia is characterised by polydipsia, polyuria, bone pain, abdominal pain, weakness, confusion, depression, renal calculi and arrhythmias. 3) This is most likely to represent uraemia. The patient has likely developed hepatorenal syndrome and has renal failure secondary to cirrhosis or marked liver dysfunction due to long-standing alcohol misuse.

stem: Theme- Rating Scales Lead In: Which of the following rating scales provide the information in the descriptions below? YBOCS YMRS 1. Which one measures severity of psychiatric symptomatology and is used in schizophrenia treatment studies? BDI HoNoS 2. Which one measures overall psychosocial functioning? GAF AUDIT ADOS 3. Which one assesses autism spectrum disorders? BPRS
correctAnswer: 1. Severity of psychiatric symptomatology - BPRS 2. Overall psychosocial functioning - GAF 3. Autism spectrum disorders - ADOS
explanation: The Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) was developed in the late 1960s as a short clinician-rated scale (based on observation) for measuring the severity of psychiatric symptomatology. It consists of 18 or 24 items, each rated on a 7-8 point scale. It covers a broad range of areas, including thought disturbance, emotional withdrawal and retardation, anxiety and depression, and hostility and suspiciousness. It has been used extensively for decades as an outcome measure in treatment studies of schizophrenia. Reliability of the BPRS is good to excellent when raters are experienced, but this is difficult to achieve without substantial training. The Global Assessment of Functioning Scale (GAF) is a rating scale measuring overall psychosocial functioning. The maximum score on the GAF is 100. The Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) is a semi-structured and lengthy diagnostic interview given by specially trained clinicians that uses standardised data to aid in diagnosis.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 34-38. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 96-98.

stem: An 8 year old child presents with sudden movements and vocalisations, as well repetitive rituals. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Tic disorders are characterised by brief, sudden, repetitive movements (motor tics) or utterances (phonic or vocal tics) that are temporarily suppressible and are usually preceded by a strong urge to perform the tic. The most common cause of childhood-onset tics is Tourette syndrome (chronic motor tic(s) and vocal tic(s)). The most common comorbidities in Tourette syndrome include ADHD, obsessive-compulsive disorder or behaviour (OCD/B) and autism spectrum disorder. Clinical features of OCD are obsessions (intrusive, repetitive, and distressing thoughts or images) and compulsions (repetitive, stereotyped, unnecessary behaviours).

stem: Which of the following is a type of narcissistic defences?
explanation: Persons with narcissistic personality disorder have a grandiose sense of self-importance; they consider themselves special and expect special treatment. They handle criticism poorly and may become enraged when someone dares criticize them, or they may appear utterly indifferent to criticism. They are commonly interpersonally exploitative, and their self-esteem is fragile. They use primitive defence mechanisms, including projection which involves attributing one’s own internal unacceptable ideas and impulses to an external target, such as another individual, and reacting accordingly to them.

stem: Cameron described the following form of thought disorder:
explanation:
Norman Cameron's analysis of formal thought disorder in 25 'unmistakably schizophrenia' patients led to the concept of asyndetic thinking that included derailment, loss of the central determining idea, and loose associations. He emphasised the lack of connections between successive thoughts in this phenomenon of ‘asyndesis’. For example, ‘I got up at eight this morning as well as few birds of different colours on the painting, shrinking all the time to drop few coins. On the floor. All the time.’ Cameron also proposed 3 other characteristic formal thought disorders – Metonymy: imprecise approximate expressions used as substitute words. For example paperskate for a pen. Overinclusion : In overinclusive thinking ideas that are only remotely related to the concept under consideration become incorporated in the patient's thinking; Conceptual boundaries are lost. Interpenetration: Irrelevant thoughts penetrate ongoing stream of thoughts.

He also described thought fragmentation, similar to Schneider's derailment concept (see below)

Carl (not Kurt) Schneider proposed a different set of 5 elements of formal thought disorder. Substitution: one thought – often inappropriate, fills the gap between other appropriate, more consistent thoughts. Omission: A chunk of thought goes missing from stream of conversation, patient being unaware – best analysed when written. Fusion: various thoughts fuse together, leading to loss of goal direction. Drivelling: disordered intermixture of constituent parts of one complex thought Derailment (aka entgleisen); In derailment normally flowing track of thoughts suddenly change. The determining tendency is preserved but is misdirected. Schneider also described desultory thinking, sometimes considered along with driveling. In desultory thinking, speech is grammatically correct but sudden ideas force their way in from time to time. Each one of these ideas is a simple thought that, if used at the right time would be quite appropriate.
reference: Jerónimo J et al. Formal Thought Disorders–Historical Roots. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2018 Nov 9;9:572.

explanation: In flight of ideas thoughts follow each other rapidly; there is no general direction of thinking; and the connections between successive thoughts appear to be due to chance factors which, however, can usually be understood. stem: In his 1987 book, Le Suicide, what did sociologist Emile Durkheim conclude?

explanation: Emile Durkheim was a French sociologist who challenged the assumption that social processes can be understood in terms of the actions of individuals and argued that even suicide, apparently the ultimately individualistic act, cannot be fully explained at the purely individual level. In his book Suicide, Durkheim used survey data purporting to show that egoistic suicide, resulting from feelings of self-reproach and sense of failure, arises from a lack of social cohesion; that altruistic suicide, carried out for the benefit of others, arises from a sense of failure to society; and that anomic suicide, arising from a sense that life is pointless, arises from an absence of social norms that he called anomie.

stem: Two medications have the same efficacy but Drug A is marketed as having a 50% failure rate whilst Drug B is marketed as having a 50% success rate. Drug B is prescribed more frequently. What is this an example of?
explanation: The framing effect is an example of cognitive bias, in which people react to a particular choice in different ways depending on how it is presented; e.g. as a loss or as a gain. It is an effect of the description, labelling, or presentation of a problem or responses to it. In this question, the two frames are merely different ways of describing the same thing. Heuristics are simple, efficient rules which people often use to form judgments and make decisions. The outcome bias is an error made in evaluating the quality of a decision when the outcome of that decision is already known. The Barnum effect is a common psychological phenomenon whereby individuals will give high accuracy ratings to descriptions of their personality that supposedly are tailored specifically to them but that are, in fact, vague and general enough to apply to a wide range of people. The Hawthorne effect is the alteration of behaviour by the subjects of a study due to their awareness of being observed.

stem: Anna is 8 years old. You are conducting some exercises to determine what stage of development she appears to be at, according to Piaget's stages of development. You present her with two glasses, both of the same shape, and both holding the same amount of orange juice. You then obtain two other glasses of different shapes: one is tall and thin, another short and broad. You pour the orange juice from one of the original glasses into the tall glass, and the juice from the other original glass into the shorter glass. You now ask Anna to tell you which glass holds the most juice. What answer indicates she has reached the concrete operational stage of development?
options: 'The short glass has the most orange juice'
'They each have more orange juice than before'
'Glasses can be half empty or half full'
'Both glasses have the same amount of orange juice'
'The tall glass has the most orange juice'
correctAnswer: 'Both glasses have the same amount of orange juice'
explanation: According to Piaget, the stage of concrete operations lasts from about 7 to 11 years of age. In this period, children operate and act on the concrete, real, and perceivable world of objects and events. Egocentric thought is replaced by operational thought, which involves dealing with a wide array of information outside the child. Children can now see things from someone else’s perspective. Children also understand the concept of conservation, which is the ability to recognise that, although the shape of objects may change, the objects still maintain or conserve other characteristics that enable them to be recognised as the same. The ability of children to understand quantity is one of Piaget’s most important cognitive developmental theories. Measures of quantity include measures of substance, length, number, liquids, and area.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 1008-1009.

stem: Which of the following of the Kohlberg's stages of moral development are paired correctly?
explanation: Lawrence Kohlberg integrated Jean Piaget’s concepts and described multiple stages of moral development within three significant levels of morality. The first level is pre-conventional morality, in which punishment and obedience are the determining factors. The second level is morality of conventional role-conformity, in which children try to conform to gain approval and maintain good relationships with others and are also guided by rigid codes of ‘law and order’ (authority orientation). The third and highest level is the morality of self-accepted moral principles (post-conventional), in which children voluntarily comply with rules based on a concept of universal ethical principles and make exceptions to rules in certain circumstances.

stem: James Williams is a 2-year-old boy who is walking confidently. When he attempts to run he falls over and becomes very tearful and upset. According to Erikson‘s Psychosocial model, which of the following crises is he most likely to be experiencing?
explanation: Erik Erikson created an original and highly influential theory of psychological development and crisis occurring in periods that extended across the entire life cycle. Stage 2 takes place from about 18 months to about 3 years. Its focus is autonomy versus shame and doubt. Erikson believed that this stage “becomes decisive for the ratio between loving goodwill and hateful self-insistence, between cooperation and willfulness, and between self-expression and compulsive self-restraint or meek compliance”. Where that ratio is favourable, the child develops an appropriate sense of autonomy and the capacity to ‘have and to hold’; where it is unfavourable, doubt and shame will undermine free will.

stem: You are working with a Child and Adolescent Mental Health team, and reading about child psychosexual development. Sigmund Freud proposed a number of concepts concerning psychosexual development. Which of the following is true regarding Freud‘s theory?

The Oedipus complex describes a boy‘s psychosexual competition with his mother for possession of his father
Between the ages of 6 and puberty, the child‘s libido is dormant
The genital and the phallic stages are interchangeable
In the oral phase the Oedipus complex comes into play
correctAnswer: Between the ages of 6 and puberty, the child‘s libido is dormant
explanation: The latency stage is the stage of relative instinctual quiescence or inactivity of sexual drive during the period from the resolution of the Oedipus complex until pubescence (from about 5-6 years until about 11-13 years). stem: Duloxetine is an antidepressant used in the UK. Which of the following is true about it?
options: Doses of 120mg are routinely used for neuropathic pain
Patients with gastric bypass surgery may need a lower dose
It is a dual action antidepressant
Smoking has no impact on the plasma levels and efficacy
It has a half-life of around 36 hours
correctAnswer: It is a dual action antidepressant
explanation:
Duloxetine, along with venlafaxine, is sometimes termed as a dual action antidepressant (acts on both serotonin and noradrenaline). The elimination half-life of duloxetine is approximately 12 hours. Usual dosage ranges are 40-60mg/day in 1-2 doses for depression, 60mg once daily for diabetic peripheral neuropathy and fibromyalgia, and 40mg twice daily for stress urinary incontinence. Studies have not demonstrated increased efficacy of duloxetine beyond 60mg/day. Some patients may require up to or more than 120mg/day, but clinical experience is quite limited with high dosing. In neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia, doses above 60mg/day have been associated with increased side effects without an increase in efficacy.

Plasma levels of duloxetine can be reduced by up to 50% in smokers (Pg 857, Maudsley 14th) and 42% lower after gastric bypass surgery (Pg 823, Maudsley 14th). Higher dose may be necessary for these patients to achieve therapeutic benefits.

stem: Pharmacokinetics in the elderly is different to those of younger individual due to the physiological changes associated with aging. Which of the following is true regarding the volume of distribution in elderly individuals?

stem: Mr. Jones visits his GP regarding his insomnia after a recent long-haul flight. His GP speaks with him and does not find any evidence of depression or other sleep disturbance. Mr. Jones is keen to try melatonin. Which one of the following statements is correct regarding the endogenous hormone melatonin?

Melatonin levels are reduced in darkness
It is produced by the pituitary
It is involved in termination of sleep
explanation: The pineal gland of the epithalamus releases melatonin, perhaps the best-known circadian modulator. Release of melatonin is dependent on environmental inputs, most notably the light cycle; melatonin increases several hours after the onset of the dark phase of the light cycle, and it remains high until the restoration of the light phase the next day (levels peak between 11pm and 3am). In humans, melatonin’s effects are the principal mediator for normal sleep onset several hours into the dark phase of the diurnal cycle. There are three types of receptors for melatonin: 1 and 2 (MT1 and MT2), which are both involved in sleep, and 3, which is actually the enzyme NRH-quinine oxidoreductase 2 and not thought to be involved in sleep physiology.

stem: Tricyclic antidepressants are recognised as being potentially hazardous in overdose, particularly when compared to newer antidepressant medications. Which of the following is true regarding tricyclics in overdose?

correctAnswer: They are subject to zero order kinetics

stem: A 50-year-old man on a neurology ward has non-dominant parietal lobe dysfunction. Identify the test that he is least likely to be able to do?
explanation: The cognitive process tested by asking the patient to copy intersecting pentagons is constructional praxis, which is a feature of non- dominant parietal lobe lesions. stem: Mr. Smith was seen by a clinical psychologist at a memory clinic and was noted to have features of executive dysfunction. Executive function is tested using which of the following tests?
explanation: The Wisconsin card sorting task is a test of executive functioning. It is a measure of problem-solving efficiency that is particularly sensitive to executive deficits of perseveration and impaired ability to flexibly generate alternative strategies in response to feedback. The patient has to determine the rule for card allocation and allocate cards accordingly. When the rule changes, a patient with frontal lobe dysfunction is likely to make more errors (tests response inhibition and set shifting).

stem: Digit span test is administered to patient with suspected cognitive impairment. This test detects problem in which of the following cognitive faculties?
explanation: Digit span is a test of working memory (immediate) and attention. Immediate (or working) memory refers to the amount of information that can be held in mind (like a phone number or digit span) to be available for immediate use. Digit span requires patients to repeat longer strings of digits increasingly as a way of assessing the ability to process relatively simple information.

stem: You are seeing a patient in a gender identity clinic. The patient would like to obtain membership of a gender that they experience, which is different from the assigned gender based on sex at birth. They are also keen to be treated as a member of the experienced gender. The most probable description when using ICD-11 nomenclature is
explanation: ICD-11 Gender Incongruence, in contrast to DSM-5 Gender Dysphoria, is explicitly not a mental disorder as it requires neither distress nor dysfunction as a feature. Notably, Gender Incongruence in Childhood and in Adolescence and Adulthood does not have the label “disorder” anymore, and are moved out of the chapter on Mental, Behavioral or Neurodevelopmental Disorders to a new ICD-11 chapter on Conditions Related to Sexual Health. Further, unlike DSM Gender Dysphoria, a 6-months duration is not required; instead 'several months' is described as a feature. Despite these differences, the commonalities between ICD-11 and DSM-5 are: (1) a strong dislike or discomfort with the one's sex characteristics, (2) a strong desire to be rid of some of all of one's sex characteristics, (3) a strong desire to have the sex characteristics of the experienced gender, and (4) a strong desire to be treated (to live and be accepted) as a person of the experienced gender.
reference:

stem: The presence of a single apolipoprotein-e4 allele increases the chance of developing Alzheimer's disease by around
explanation: A polymorphism in the Apolipoprotein ε4 (Chromosome 19) is a major risk factor for late- onset Alzheimer disease. Specifically, the presence of ε4 alleles increases risk of late-onset AD; people with one copy of the gene (ε3/4 heterozygotes) have 3x the incidence of Alzheimer’s disease than no ε4 gene, and people with two ε4 genes have the disease 8 times more frequently than do those with no ε4 gene (some quote a higher risk); genetic testing for presence of ε4 is not currently recommended as it is also present in people without dementia, and not found in all cases of dementia. This gene promotes the deposition of beta-amyloid protein in the brain, contributing to the formation of senile plaques. In most populations, the ε3 allele is the most common. However, in familial late-onset Alzheimer disease, the incidence of ε4 is approximately 50%, compared with 16% in normal controls. The ancestral allele ε2, in contrast, is underrepresented. Epidemiological studies suggest that 30-60% of late-onset Alzheimer disease cases have at least one ε4 allele. The ε4 genotype appears to be a more important risk factor for Alzheimer disease in populations of European and Asian origin when compared with populations of African origin.
reference: Fernandez CG, Hamby ME, McReynolds ML, Ray WJ. The role of APOE4 in disrupting the homeostatic functions of astrocytes and microglia in aging and Alzheimer’s disease. Frontiers in aging neuroscience. 2019 Feb 11;11:14.

stem: Social anxiety and gaze avoidance are features of which of the following trinucleotide expansion syndrome?
explanation: Fragile X syndrome is associated with a trinucleotide (CGG) triplet repeat on the distal part of the long arm of the X chromosome (Xq27.3- FMR1) that leads to the characteristic ‘fragile’ appearance of the chromosome. FMR1 gene is required for normal neural development; penetrance is low, but greater in males than females (due to the protective effects of the second normal X chromosome in females). Behavioural features are similar to those seen in ADHD and autism and include hand flapping/waving, repetitive mannerisms, shyness, gaze avoidance, poor peer relationships, communication difficulties (e.g. delayed language development, conversational rigidity, perseveration, echolalia, palilalia(repetition of syllables, words, phrases), cluttering, and over-detailed speech), and psychiatric problems (e.g. prominent depression/anxiety).

stem: Which one of the following is a primary proponent of endophenotypes concept?
explanation: Having broken new ground in the field of polygenicity and epigenetics, Irving Gottesman understood that unraveling the complex genomic basis of the fuzzy and qualitative diagnosis of schizophrenia would be a daunting task. How to make the task simpler, more parsimonious, and more neurobiologically meaningful? To do this, Gottesman introduced the concept of endophenotypes into the schizophrenia literature. Endophenotypes are laboratory-based measures that show deficits in schizophrenia patients and lesser deficits in their first-degree ‘unaffected’ relatives and are viewed as being more proximal to genes and having a simpler genetic architecture than are ‘fuzzy’ qualitative diagnostic disorders.
reference: Braff DL, Tamminga CA. Endophenotypes, epigenetics, polygenicity and more: Irv Gottesman’s dynamic legacy. Schizophrenia bulletin. 2017 Jan 1;43(1):10-6.

stem: The process of meiosis produces
explanation: Meiosis is a form of cell division in which the nucleus divides into four daughter nuclei, each containing half the chromosomes of the parent nucleus. It consists of two consecutive divisions: during the first, homologous chromosomes pair up, exchange genetic material by crossing over (‘recombination’), then during the anaphase part of the cycle move apart by disjunction to form separate haploid nuclei. During the second phase, these daughter nuclei divide by mitosis (with a further anaphase), producing four haploid cells.
reference: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4 th Edition. 2015.

stem: Which of the following is best termed as an intermediate phenotype with high occurrence in relatives but cannot be justifiably classified as an endophenotype for schizophrenia?
explanation: Predominantly, neurological soft signs (NSS) have been looked at as endophenotypes (i.e., hardcopies of the genetic liability) and thus a trait phenomenon. However, the literature on NSS in schizophrenia presents at least partially diverging results. On the one hand, research speaks in favour of NSS as being a stable entity (i.e., a trait): NSS are more pronounced in patients compared to their relatives; they are present at disease onset; there is a relationship with the most stable symptoms, namely negative and cognitive ones. On the other hand, there are arguments supporting a fluctuating aspect, especially of motor signs. Only the presence of a trait can be used as an endophenotype or a predictor, but not the quantitative expression (i.e., the state). Thus, the usage of NSS as an endophenotype has to be called into question. The most established endophenotypes for schizophrenia are changes in neurocognition (attention deficits, working and verbal declarative memory dysfunctions) and neurophysiology (pre-pulse inhibition, anti-saccade impairment, event-related potential deficits) (Donati et al., 2020).
reference: Bachmann S, Schröder J. Neurological soft signs in schizophrenia: an update on the state-versus trait-perspective. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2018 Jan 8;8:272. Donati FL, D’Agostino A, Ferrarelli F. Neurocognitive and neurophysiological endophenotypes in schizophrenia: An overview. Biomarkers in Neuropsychiatry. 2020 Dec 1;3:100017.

stem: The Kluver-Bucy syndrome is typically associated with lesions of which of the following structures?
explanation: In 1937, Heinrich Kluver and Paul Bucy described a dramatic behavioural syndrome in monkeys after bilateral temporal lobectomy. The full Kluver-Bucy syndrome (KBS) – hyperorality, placidity, hypermetamorphosis, dietary changes, altered sexual behaviour, and visual agnosia – is evident within 3 weeks following operation. By the 1970s, it was clear that the major symptoms of KBS are produced by destroying either the temporal neocortex or the amygdala bilaterally. The clinical features of KBS in humans are similar to those in monkeys, but the full syndrome is rarely seen, probably because the anterior temporal lobe dysfunction is usually less severe than that following total temporal lobe ablation in monkeys.
reference: Lanska DJ. The Klüver-Bucy syndrome. Neurologic-Psychiatric Syndromes in Focus-Part I. 2018;41:77-89.

stem: The enzyme involved in degradation of noradrenaline in presynaptic neurons is
explanation: Norepinephrine (NE) action is terminated by two principal destructive or catabolic enzymes that turn NE into inactive metabolites. The first is monoamine oxidase A or B, which is located in mitochondria in the presynaptic neuron and elsewhere. The second is catechol-O- methyltransferase (COMT), which is thought to be located largely outside of the presynaptic nerve terminal. The action of NE can be terminated not only by enzymes that destroy NE, but also by a transport pump for NE that removes it from acting in the synapse without destroying it. That transport pump is sometimes called the ‘NE transporter’ or ‘NET’ and sometimes the ‘NE reuptake pump’.
reference: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5 th Edition. 2021. pp. 253-254.

stem: Which of the following pathological bodies is made up of ubiquitin and alpha synuclein and is associated with loss of dopaminergic neurons in basal ganglia?
explanation: The key constituent of Lewy bodies is alpha-synuclein. When aggregates of misfolded, overexpressed alpha-synuclein accumulate in neurons or surrounding glial cells, Lewy bodies are formed. Lewy bodies are immunoreactive for alpha-synuclein as well as for ubiquitin and alpha- beta-crystallin. Neuropathic changes of dementia with Lewy bodies include the presence of Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites in the cerebral cortex as well as in the brainstem. These are often accompanied by some degree of Alzheimer disease neuropathologic changes, often with a moderate beta-amyloid plaque burden but relatively lower tangle burden.
reference: Sanford AM. Lewy body dementia. Clinics in geriatric medicine. 2018 Nov 1;34(4):603-15. Gray F, Duyckaerts C, de Girolami U. Escourolle and Poirier’s Manual of Basic Neuropathology, 6 th Edition. 2019. pp. 6-7, 197.

stem: A 55 year old lady presents with weakness of her legs and hands. She feels clumsy with a history of falls. On examination she has fasciculations in her tongue and memory deficits. She is diagnosed to have amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The primary pathological change will be noted in
explanation: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is characterised by degeneration of both upper motor neurons (UMNs) and lower motor neurons (LMNs). While the balance between the severity and pace of involvement of these two sets of neurons may vary from case to case, the combination is characteristic of ALS. In many cases, the disease begins with involvement of spinal LMNs, manifesting as weakness in the arms or legs. In others, ALS begins with bulbar symptoms and may be termed progressive bulbar palsy.
